claims.text: A machine-learning potential trained on strategically sampled ab initio data can accurately predict the free energies of both solid and liquid phases in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The proposed machine-learning potential can predict high-temperature thermodynamic properties in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The method will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The method will substantially reduce computational cost relative to TOR-TILD.
The proposed applicability range comprises systems containing 3–10 elements.
The proposed temperature range near fusion is approximately 0.8 Tm to 1.2 Tm.
The method may apply from room temperature to several thousand kelvin when both solid and liquid phases are well defined.
The model's representation of local atomic environments can capture vibrational-entropy contributions.
The model's representation of local atomic environments can capture anharmonic effects.
The model's representation of local atomic environments can capture electron–vibration coupling.
Training on a strategically selected subset of high-fidelity ab initio data allows the potential to approximate the free-energy landscapes of solid and liquid states.
Approximating the phase free-energy landscapes with the machine-learning potential reduces the need for full-scale ab initio molecular dynamics while retaining near-ab initio accuracy.
The proposed method is expected to provide approximately a tenfold or greater speedup over explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method is expected to provide approximately a tenfold or greater speedup over TOR-TILD.
Predicted phase free energies are expected to deviate by no more than approximately 5% from benchmark values.
Predicted fusion enthalpies and melting temperatures are expected to deviate by no more than approximately 5% from benchmark values.
Successful application depends on the ab initio training set adequately covering the relevant configurational space.
Systems with extreme anharmonicity or unusual electronic effects may require additional validation.
Prior elemental and binary results provide promising evidence for similar machine-learning approaches.
